title: Five ways to cut mosquitoes in a Houston yard
excerpt: Most mosquitoes biting you were born within a few hundred feet of your back door. Here's how to take away the places they breed.
content:
Houston's mosquitoes don't fly far. The ones in your yard almost always grew up in standing water close by, often on your own property.

Tip out standing water every week

Plant saucers, toys, tarps and birdbaths all hold enough water for mosquitoes to breed. A quick walk round the yard each weekend breaks the cycle.

Clear your gutters

Leaves block gutters and leave shallow pools that stay wet for days after a storm. Clean them in spring and again in fall.

Trim back shady plants

Adult mosquitoes rest in cool, damp shade during the day. Thinning dense shrubs near the patio leaves them fewer places to hide.

Fix leaky hoses and outdoor taps

A slow drip onto the same patch of ground keeps it muddy all summer.

Treat what you can't remove

For the spots you can't change, a monthly barrier treatment from April to October keeps numbers down. Ask us about a yard visit.

title: Six signs you may have termites (and what to do next)
excerpt: Termites can work inside a wall for years before anyone notices. These are the early signs worth checking for each spring.
content:
Texas has some of the busiest termite seasons in the country, and most homeowners only find out when the damage is done. A few minutes of checking each spring can save thousands.

Mud tubes on the foundation

Subterranean termites build pencil-wide tunnels of mud up the slab or piers to reach the wood. Look along the outside of the house and in the garage.

Swarms and dropped wings

In spring, winged termites swarm near windows and lights. Piles of small, equal-sized wings on a sill are a strong sign.

Wood that sounds hollow

Tap baseboards and door frames. Termites eat wood from the inside, so damaged boards sound papery.

Doors and windows that stick

Moisture from termite activity can warp frames, so a door that suddenly sticks is worth a look.

Tiny pellets

Drywood termites push out droppings that look like coarse sand or coffee grounds.

What to do next

Don't spray store-bought products into the area; it scatters the colony. Book a free inspection and we'll tell you what's there and what it will cost to treat.

title: Why fire ant mounds pop up after rain
excerpt: Every big storm brings a new crop of mounds across Houston lawns. Here's what's going on and how to deal with them safely.
content:
Fire ants don't arrive with the rain. They were already under your lawn. When the soil floods, they build their mounds up higher to keep the colony dry.

Don't kick or rake the mound

Disturbing a mound sends hundreds of ants out to sting. It also makes the colony move a few feet away and start again.

Use bait, not just contact sprays

Sprays kill the ants you can see. Bait is carried down to the queen, which is what actually ends the colony. Spread it on dry grass in the evening when ants are feeding.

Treat the whole yard twice a year

A broadcast treatment in spring and fall keeps new queens from settling in. It works far better than chasing single mounds.

Keep kids and pets clear

Mark mounds with a flag until they're gone, and call us if someone is stung many times or has a reaction.

title: How to keep mice and rats out this winter
excerpt: When the nights get cool, mice and rats look for a warm way in. Most homes have more open doors than their owners know.
content:
A mouse can fit through a gap the size of a dime, and a rat through a hole the size of a quarter. Closing those gaps does more than any trap.

Walk round the outside

Check where pipes, cables and AC lines enter the house. Fill gaps with steel wool and seal over it with caulk.

Look at the garage door

Worn rubber seals at the bottom of garage doors are the most common way in that we find. They're cheap to replace.

Cut back trees and vines

Roof rats climb. Branches touching the roof and vines on the walls give them a road to the attic.

Store food in hard containers

Pet food and birdseed in paper bags are an open invitation. Move them into sealed bins.

Listen for scratching

Noises in the attic or walls at night mean they're already in. Our rodent service seals entry points and removes what's inside, with a follow-up visit included.
